newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish debt seen profiting little from March CPI.
newsitem.headline: Spanish debt seen profiting little from March CPI.

text.p: The Spanish debt market is unlikely to draw any further strength from an expected fall in inflation on Friday, given uncertainty hanging over international markets, analysts said on Thursday.

Spain's debt market succumbed to heavy profit-taking on Thursday, backpedalling a bit after a week of large gains on improved European single currency prospects, expectations of falling inflation and an official rate cut.

"Markets went from an excess of optimism in January to an excess of pessimism in February and March. This week optimism seemed back. But..I'd say these levels are about right," said Jose Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
At 1300 GMT the long-term bond future was trading down 56 basis points to 112.92, after having climbed to 113.50 on Wednesday's close from 110.56 one week before.
Last weekend's European Union finance ministers' meeting backed some market participants' views that the single currency would start on time.

Domestically, the market was gaining ground ahead of Friday's March consumer price data release. The market expects a further inflation decline which the Bank of Spain might back with an official rate cut as soon as April 15.
"The Spanish market has gained a lot in recent days, now it's correcting a bit," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
March CPI, to be announced on Friday, is expected to show a year-on-year increase of 2.4 percent, down from February's 2.5 percent and from January's 2.9 percent.
Any bigger fall is expected to prompt the Bank of Spain to make its third rate cut this year, analysts agreed.
"The inflation trend in coming months will allow further reduction in interest rates," said Antonio Garcia Rebollar, director at Renta 4.
"We do not rule out a March yearly rate at 2.1 or 2.2 percent," he added.
There are analysts thinking even less than that would be enough for the Bank of Spain.
"A CPI at 2.3 percent could prompt the Bank of Spain to cut rate. If it's not the case there's still room for cuts in the future," said Gwyn Hacche at HSBC in London.
A further reduction in the 5.75 percent key money market rate is expected to boost the short end of the Spanish market, whose yields curve steepened already in anticipation.
The spread between two- and 10-year bonds was trading at around 127 basis points on Thursday from 120 on Monday.
But analysts were casting doubts over the long end reaction.
"In recent days we had a correction, but the main trend remains down, not on the upside. And it'll resume soon," said Gregorio Gomez at All Trading in Madrid.

"Short run much of the peripheral markets' trend will depend on the dollar. If it rises more, we may get expectations of Germany raising its rates and this will affect Spain and Italy a lot," HSBC's Hacche said.
The U.S. dollar was trading at its daily low versus the yen after having hit a 56-month high, and also slipped against the mark after a 37-month high overnight.
--Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
